fact: In 1867 Tom Allen seconded Tom Kelly of Baltimore against Billy Parkinson at Acquia Creek, agreed to help Kelly's backers, and cut the ropes so Kelly's crowd could rush the ring; the referee awarded the fight to Parkinson on a foul.
In 1867 Tom Allen was about 5 feet 10 inches tall and weighed about 164 pounds.
Tom Allen was one of Jimmy Elliott's seconds when Elliott fought Charley Gallagher on Peche Island in the Detroit River on November 12, 1868; after 21 rounds the referee decided for Elliott.
Charles Convy Gallagher, a Cleveland fighter, was described as a warm friend of Tom Allen in December 1868.
Bill Ryall signed the articles of agreement for Tom Allen's fight with Bill Davis, with Harry Slade and Bill Ryall as Allen's friends at the making of the match.
Tom Allen trained for his fight with Bill Davis in December 1868; Davis's fighting weight was 185 pounds, and Allen would not carry so much weight.
On Christmas night 1868 men said to be Allen's backers confronted Bill Davis at Doyle's near the Fair Grounds, and one of them cut Davis's wrist with a knife.
In January 1869 Tom Allen trained on the Gravois road, about nine miles from St. Louis, under Tom Kelly.
Tom Allen fought Bill Davis on January 12, 1869, with Bill Ryall and Tom Kelly as his seconds, and collected a contribution of about $150 for Davis after the fight.
On the boat back from the Davis fight on January 12, 1869, Tom Allen and Charles Gallagher nearly fought in the cabin until the crowd kept them apart.
Tom Allen fought Charlie Gallagher on February 23, 1869, seconded by Patsy Reardon and Jack Looney, with Dan Ryan as umpire; Allen was reported to have said he was England's champion.
In May 1869 Tom Allen went into training under Sherman Thurston, and his weight was printed in garbled form (probably 165 pounds).
A full-length portrait of Tom Allen, the renowned pugilist, was made by a photographer in June 1869.
Tom Keho acted for Mike McCoole and Billy Carroll acted for Tom Allen at a final deposit on June 8, 1869.
Tom Allen was invited to the Laclede Jockey Club races with his trainers and would probably attend the last day.
The preliminaries of the Allen and McCoole match were arranged on July 9, 1869 at Hennessy's saloon, with Tom Kelley appearing for Mike McCoole.
Jim Coyne was Tom Allen's mentor in July 1869.
Tom Allen fought Charley Gallagher on August 17, 1869, under American colors; afterwards Gallagher struck at him spitefully as Allen went to shake hands, and the outcome was disputed.
Tom Allen made a speech of thanks to his hearers at a reception in September 1869.
Tom Allen and Jim Coyne were to be present at a deposit on October 9, 1869.
Tom Allen had numerous friends in Cincinnati, judging by the tone of the Cincinnati press.
Tom Allen had a row with Sherman Thurston at the Buckeye House in Cincinnati on October 31, 1869; the Enquirer says it was settled with a drink and a handshake.
In November 1869 Tom Allen's backers rejected Mike McCoole's choice of stakeholder, Murray, and Bill Carroll and Mr. Thorweger of St. Louis went to Cincinnati to settle the dispute.
On December 1, 1869 Tom Allen said Mike McCoole was very good as a private citizen but stood No. 3 as a fighter, and Billy Carroll was authorized to make all arrangements for Allen's fights.
Referee Eph Holland of Boston was said to have been fixed to give Joe Goss the decision, and Fred Watkins, Allen's backer, lost $1,000 to him.
On 25 January 1870 Tom Allen seconded George Seddons, with Patsey Curtin, against John Lafferty at Carroll Island, Illinois, and took charge of Seddons before the fight.
On 25 January 1870 Tom Allen seconded George Carey, with Patsey Curtin, against James C. Gallagher at Carroll Island, Illinois, and threw up the sponge for Carey, who was beaten in 18 minutes.
In March 1870, before his fight with Jem Mace, Tom Allen's St. Louis friends said he would beat Mace, and Allen and Mace traded remarks in the newspapers.
Tom Allen trained at the Wash House for his fight with Jem Mace in spring 1870.
A championship belt from Allen's St. Louis friends was to be presented to him at his benefit in April 1870, and Mrs. Allen took it with her after the Mace fight.
Jack Looney predicted, about a week before the Mace fight, that Allen would be defeated because he was not in proper condition.
Joe Coburn and Sherman Thurston seconded Tom Allen in his fight with Jem Mace on 10 May 1870.
Tom Allen weighed about 175 pounds on the day of the Mace fight.
On the day of the Mace fight Billy Carroll accepted John C. Heenan's proposal of Rufus Hunt as referee, and told the crowd that Allen had never had a fair show.
Mike McCoole and Tom Allen had bets on the Mace fight.
Tom Allen got half the excursion money from the Mace fight and had to split it with his backers Billy Carroll and John Franklin.
On the night of the Mace fight Tom Allen played the piano with both hands.
Dr. Morse said a $1,000 premium at an agricultural fair might bring Tom Allen or Mike McCoole to a prize fight.
In August 1870 Tom Allen backed Punch Morris in a $100 fight against Steve O'Donnell, and Morris was quartered at the Wash Home to be trained by Allen's trainer.
In October 1870 Allen eased his training after a report that Gallagher was sick, and betting was two to one with few willing to back Gallagher.
Tom Allen bet $1,000 to $600 that he could whip the winner of the Owen Meekin and James C. Gallagher match.
Tom Allen's fight with Gallagher took place in early November 1870, with Barney Aaron and George Collins as his seconds, and afterwards Allen gave $50 of a $100 subscription to Gallagher.
A garbled June 1871 report seems to place Tom Allen at the ring where Jem Mace was sitting.
In June 1871 Tom Allen was to train Jem Mace four miles from St. Louis and back him against Ned O'Baldwin.
Tom Allen seconded Jem Mace at the Mace-Coburn fight near New Orleans on 30 November 1871, and was among the prize-ring notables present.
On 21 August 1872 Tom Allen waited at the telegraph office for news of a reported Mace and O'Baldwin fight, and later said O'Baldwin was too much for Mace.
Tom Allen and Mike McCoole quarrelled at Jack Looney's New Year's fancy ball at about 4 a.m. on January 2, 1873.

Before the McCoole fight in 1873 Tom Allen stayed at home reducing to 170 pounds by longer walks and did not go into training quarters for nearly two months; in August he was reported to have done little training.
In June 1873 a Democrat reporter asked Tom Allen whether he was afraid of Mike McCoole, and Allen said he was more afraid of his wife, especially when he came home late at night.
Allen's emissaries said that when Allen called on McCoole the previous Sunday, McCoole kept out of his way.
While preparing for the McCoole fight in August 1873, Tom Allen said he would then be ready for Charley Gallagher or any other man.
Tom Allen was present at the fourth deposit at McCoole's saloon on August 5, 1873.
Tom Allen did not appear at the final deposit for the McCoole fight on September 2, 1873.
Tom Allen fought Mike McCoole on September 23, 1873, with Arthur Chambers and Patsy Shepherd among his seconds.
F. C. Cox won over $102 betting on Tom Allen on September 23, 1873.
Tom Allen received half of the $12,000 boat money from his second fight with Mike McCoole.
On the return trip from the McCoole fight Tom Allen started a subscription for Mike McCoole, headed with $100, and the money was given to the trainers Madden and Tricks.
Tom Allen said on September 25, 1873 that he planned to enjoy himself for two weeks and then return to training.
Mike McCoole was described as Tom Allen's opponent in October 1873.
John Looney suspected that Ben Hogan had arranged the failed excursion as a put-up job to avoid meeting Tom Allen.

Before the Ben Hogan fight Tom Allen had not begun training and would start only a few days before the contest; by October 7 he was reported to be already in trim while Hogan was still getting in trim.
The odds favored Tom Allen over Ben Hogan, in some cases two to one, and a bet of two hundred against one was placed with Joel Herbert.
Arthur Chambers was one of Tom Allen's seconds in the Ben Hogan fight at East St. Louis.
Tom Allen denied fouling Ben Hogan after Dr. C. E. Tennent certified that Hogan was struck below the belt.

At the 1874 Springfield reunion a pickpocket reached for Tom Allen's pocket while Allen sat in the second gallery with a friend; Allen caught the pickpocket's hand and squeezed it, and the victim's outcry was the first alarm of a panic in the gallery.

Tom Allen said in February 1874 that he sided with the legislature's bill against prize-fighting because the ring had become corrupt, and that the bill had put his name in to mark him, while the Times had called him a refugee, which he denied.
Tom Allen was one of Edwards' seconds in Edwards' fight with Collyer near Pittsburg in August 1874.
Fred Watkins furnished something for Tom Allen about 1875, according to a retrospective account that is garbled ('Allen's apg').

At the Comique benefit on January 21, 1875 Tom Allen came on stage wearing his champion's belt to loud applause and, at the audience's demand, sang three or four songs although he was not on the bill as a singer.
Arthur Chambers, champion of the lightweights, put up $250 as a binder for Tom Allen in the hands of Harry Gill for the Rooke match.
Tom Allen said he weighed 210 pounds (printed as '3i0') and had to train down before the Rooke fight.
The silver goblet presented to Tom Allen held a quart and cost $250.

The first Allen-Rooke match fell apart in June 1875 over the stakes: John Chamberlain, chosen as final stakeholder and accepting on June 1, declined at the eleventh hour because some of his friends had money on Rooke and wanted their stakes back, and Shaughnessy, one of Rooke's backers, put an attachment on the stakes held by Harry Hill.

After the Rooke match broke down, Harry Hill returned the $3,000 stakes from the first match and kept $1,000 of Allen's money to post for a new contest; Jem Coyne of Newark wrote to Allen planning another match with Rooke and asking Allen to second him, and Allen said the new arrangements were news to him and that Hill was authorized to act for him.

In December 1875 Tom Allen was reported to be preparing for the stage: a rumour said he would make a debut in St. Louis in an American drama written for him, and a later report said he was to appear in a sensational play written for him, playing a rough diamond who rescues the heroine, under the supervision of a leading actress.
In 1876 Tom Allen had about $25,000 but lost most of it making a book in England.

Tom Allen held over $600 in stakes on the Carteron-Rigal wrestling match and refereed it at the Theatre Comique, St. Louis, on February 8, 1876, where it went undecided after a severe struggle; he ruled that the final decision would come on Thursday evening, February 10.
Tom Allen played a legitimate part in the crib scene from Tom and Jerry at the Theatre Comique, St. Louis, a couple of weeks before April 1876.

Friends of Tom Allen met to raise money to buy back the belt won from Mike McCoole and present it to him at his benefit on March 30, 1876; Theobald Bauer and Andre Christol volunteered to wrestle there for a massive silver goblet from Allen, with Wilhelm Beyer to referee.
Tom Allen objected when Joe Coburn was billed in St. Louis as the Champion of the World.

Tom Allen introduced Prof. Bauer and Herr Heygster to the audience at the Temple, St. Louis, before their second wrestling match on April 8, 1876, and during the recess announced that a silver belt, obtained by Bauer's friends for Bauer as champion Greco-Roman wrestler of America, would be presented to Bauer.
Tom Allen received a dispatch from Jem Coyne of Newark, N.J., announcing that Joe Goss had arrived in America.

Tom Allen was a guest, with Prof. Bauer, Andre Christol and Leon Schuler, at a breakfast given by the French caterer Jean Bonnet in St. Louis on April 10, 1876, where Bauer said he would return to St. Louis and make a match with Julius Schroeder once Allen notified him that a suitable deposit had been posted.
Tom Allen said he knocked Ned Donnelly down on Tuesday, April 11, 1876, after Donnelly sneered when Allen asked whether he would break their engagement.

Tom Allen appeared for the wrestler Bauer and put up his $250 deposit for Bauer's wrestling match with Julius Schroeder at the Temple, and on May 4, 1876 at Tony Faust's he deposited the remainder of the stakes and was empowered to sign articles of agreement for the match.

Tom Allen was chosen referee for the wrestling match between Thiebaud Bauer and Julius Schroeder at the Temple, and on May 6, 1876 he came on stage with the lightweight champions Arthur Chambers and Billy Edwards and introduced them to the audience.
Ben De Bar stood by Tom Allen at a signing on May 12, 1876 and put up Allen's money.
In July 1876 Tom Allen trained at Cedar Park, a retreat near Carthage owned by John Young, under the care of Jack Madden, and began active training on the Monday before an interview.
Joe Goss said the coming fight with Tom Allen would be one of the hardest ever known in the annals of the ring.

Tom Allen published an apology to the New York Clipper in August 1876 for the unjust criticism he had written; the Clipper had excluded his name from its columns for nearly four years after a card he wrote.
Tom Allen refereed the Bauer-Miller wrestling match at Wood's Theater in Cincinnati on August 29, 1876.

Before the Joe Goss fight, Eph Holland was in charge of the affair, Dad Ryan acted as Allen's umpire and Jack Brown as Goss's, and Joe Goss offered $1,000 on the result; Allen covered a $1,000 wager from Goss, and Fred Watkins, backing Allen, handed a $1,000 bill to referee Holland, who had made himself stakeholder.

On the day of the Joe Goss fight Tom Allen weighed 174 pounds to Goss's 165; Tom Kelly and Arthur Chambers were Allen's seconds, and Jack Looney arrived in Cincinnati with a party of 25 men, saying Allen must be whipped.

Tom Allen said he had put up his own stake money for the Goss fight and believed Eph Holland had used it against him, and that in a fair fight he could have beaten Joe Goss in half an hour; in a card he wrote, he said it was impossible to obtain fair play in this country.
On September 11, 1876 Tom Allen made the rounds of the Cincinnati hotels and then went into a saloon on Vine Street near Fourth Street while crowds waited outside.
Tom Allen weighed about 180 pounds after the Goss fight.
Tom Allen claimed in March 1877 that he could beat Joe Goss.
Pat Mullins and J. Driscoll were Tom Allen's seconds in his glove fight with Tompkins Gilbert in October 1877.
In March 1878 Tom Allen was in training at Barnet, on the Thames near London, under his trainer Jack Hopkins, weighing fourteen stone (196 pounds).
It was alleged that Tom Allen's welching was the direct cause of an assault on him in Cork in January 1882.
In January 1882 private advices said Tom Allen's American property had vanished and that he had gone to the dogs through dissipation.
Billy Madden said Tom Allen was a first-class man and hard hitter, but that John L. Sullivan could have beaten him in his prime.
Tom Allen called Tug Wilson a faker for skipping out on his backer, Richard K. Fox.
Tom Allen said he had never met John L. Sullivan but judged him, from his record, the best man in the world.
The Boston Star described Tom Allen as a perfect gentleman and a credit to his profession.
Tom Allen said he had not come to America to fight anyone.
Tom Allen's silver cup was displayed on Mr. Shepherd's sideboard at the Abbey in Boston in November 1882.
At an exhibition on November 27, 1882, John L. Sullivan came onto the stage to deny he was afraid of Tom Allen, and the two shook hands.
After Tom Allen's November 1882 exhibition, R. K. Fox decided not to back him any further, and the $1,000 posted on Allen's behalf was recovered from Harry Hill's.

In December 1882 the Parson and others spread the report that Tom Allen was on a big spree and had become a total wreck, and Allen said Joe Elliott of the New York Herald had started the story that he was played out.
Tom Allen acted as umpire for Theobald Bauer in his Greco-Roman wrestling match with Muldoon at Masonic Hall, St. Louis, on January 27, 1883.
Tom Allen was to referee a 135-yard handicap sprint at Sportsman's Park on Sunday, January 28, 1883.
It was rumored that Tom Allen had received a dispatch from Billy Madden asking him to select training quarters for Charley Mitchell, who was matched to fight Slade.
Tom Allen said he had never heard of Booth in connection with racing, but believed he was a fancy rider.
Tom Allen judged Charley Mitchell the coming man after Mitchell's sparring exhibition with Billy Madden at the People's Theatre, St. Louis.
A couple of thugs jumped Tom Allen and tried to rob him because they thought he was no good.
A rumor that Tom Allen had become stiff and short of wind was bringing him more business.
Tom Allen, shown a report of a fight at Caldwell, Idaho, said he knew neither pugilist and discredited the account of Martland being badly beaten.

Tom Allen confronted John L. Sullivan behind the footlights of the People's Theatre in St. Louis on May 8, 1884 over Sullivan's remarks about Zachritz, and a row seemed imminent until friends hustled them apart.

Tom Allen and Tom Kelly handled the Union Club tournament in St. Louis in June and July 1884: entries could be made at Allen's after noon on June 25, and the two umpired the boxing at the Union Club athletic sports on July 4.
Tom Allen predicted that John L. Sullivan would knock out Dominick McCaffery in one round if the police let the fight go on.
In a race-track gag, Tom Allen, the ex-champion pugilist, was 'knocked out in the first round' at the Fair Grounds track, meaning he had lost his bets.
Tom Allen acted as second for Ed Kelly in the four-round contest against Jack Burke at the Casino Theater, St. Louis, on January 8, 1886.
Tom Allen bet on the horse Cuban Queen at the St. Louis races on June 15, 1886, because her father was named Strathmore.
Tom Allen backed Antonio Pierre in a private catch-as-catch-can wrestling match against Greek George on August 2, 1886, and Greek George beat Pierre in two falls.
George LaBlanche arrived in St. Louis in October 1886 and visited Tom Allen and Tom Kelly.

In January 1887 Tom Allen said he was in correspondence with Jem Smith, who had told him he would not fight Sullivan east of Omaha, and Allen said a Smith-Sullivan fight could only be for the championship under London prize-ring rules.
Tom Allen was named with Tom Kelly as a teacher who could teach St. Louis youngsters boxing.
Tom Allen was one of Ed Kelly's seconds when Kelly fought Dan Daly at Hurricane, Missouri, on April 26, 1887, and Daly defeated Kelly.
Tom Allen said that Smith would beat Kilrain and would whip Sullivan if they ever met.
Newspapers had written that Sherman Thurston was Tom Allen's trainer, but the Globe-Democrat said Thurston never was and that Allen was afraid of him.
Tom Allen declared that Mace's success was chiefly due to his left hand, which never failed to land where he wanted it to do execution.
Tom Allen, among other local authorities, was of the opinion that Kilrain could whip Sullivan under prize-ring rules.
Tom Allen was timekeeper at the Standard when D. McMillan stayed fifteen minutes with Muldoon at Greco-Roman wrestling.
Tom Allen seconded Arthur Flint in Flint's prize fight against Hugh McManus near St. Clair, Missouri, on April 16, 1888, and threw up the sponge for Flint to end the fight.
Tom Allen was in a street fight with Dan Daly at Seventh and Market streets, St. Louis, on June 17, 1888.
Tom Allen was one of five prize-fighters whom Dr. Mathew D. Field brought before the New York Neurological Society in October 1888 to have their ears examined.

Tom Allen made a wager with Dan Daly on October 16, 1888, on a gloved match between Daly and Hugh McManus set for December 1888, and in December backed McManus and claimed a $750 forfeit, interfering with the fight.
Tom Allen backed Jake Kilrain against John L. Sullivan before their July 1889 fight at Richburg, and was at the ringside when they fought.
Edward Smith was to be Tom Allen's guest for a few days in April 1890.
Tom Allen wrote that a Sioux boxer would be unlikely to become a pugilist and would kick and bite like a savage once he began to take punishment.
Tom Allen preferred Peter Maher to Bob Fitzsimmons in March 1892, tried unsuccessfully to place money on Maher before their fight, and said he saw the Fitzsimmons-Maher fight.
On March 2, 1892, Tom Allen accompanied Charley Mitchell into the ring at the Olympic Club in New Orleans, with Frank Slavin and Pat Allen, before Mitchell's sparring bout.

On March 5, 1892, Tom Allen was at the Southern Hotel in New Orleans, waiting there to take Frank Slavin out, and was in Charley Mitchell's room when Mitchell dictated his reply to John L. Sullivan's challenge.
Tom Allen held his birthday celebration with friends at his headquarters on Market Street, St. Louis, on April 23, 1892.
In May 1892 Tom Allen was a Frank Slavin man, and he wanted to place money on Slavin to win, being more positive than Kelly that Slavin would be the victor.

Tom Allen was at the ringside in New Orleans on September 5, 1892, for the McAuliffe-Myer fight, one of the two most noted St. Louisans present, and Fred Watkins was in the St. Louis delegation there.

Tom Allen and Tom Kelly backed John L. Sullivan before the September 1892 New Orleans fights, and after Sullivan lost to Corbett on September 7, 1892, Allen said Sullivan was unfit and overweight and that Corbett won squarely.
The Post-Dispatch answered a reader that Tom Allen never fought Jem Mace.
Tom Allen said he would see that Frank 'Dutch' Neil's stake was posted for a proposed finish fight with Johnnie Daly in November 1892.
Tom Allen received a letter from Charley Mitchell, dated London, November 7, 1892, about Mitchell's coming fight with Corbett.
Ed Smith, the Denver heavyweight, and his brother Paddy spent a few days with Tom Allen in December 1892.
A New York writer said Joe Goddard was no more a prize fighter in the modern sense than Tom Allen was.
Tom Allen picked Ed Smith to beat Joe Goddard, backed him and won heavily on the bet, and was one of Smith's seconds at the New Orleans fight on 3 March 1893, which Smith fairly won.
In October 1893 Tom Allen said Charlie Mitchell must beat Jim Corbett.

Tom Allen was stakeholder for the Sharpe-Crosby fight and held the $1,000 posted by the backers, and he suggested the Armourdale Club postpone the fight from 21 November to the first week of December so Sharpe could get in condition.
In December 1893 Tom Allen was confident Corbett would meet his conqueror in Charley Mitchell, and said Corbett's battles with Jackson and Sullivan showed him to be a very ordinary fighter.
Tom Allen made an ox-tail jelly to harden Charley Mitchell's stomach before his fight with Corbett, sent it to Mitchell's training quarters, and offered Paddy Smith $100 for the receipt for it.
Tom Allen was to prepare Mitchell's food and may have been one of his seconds; he assisted in Mitchell's training and was one of his seconds at the Corbett-Mitchell fight in Florida in January 1894.
In January 1894 Tom Allen spent much of his time on the beach or at the top of the old Anastasia lighthouse, a stone's throw from Mitchell's cottage.

Tom Allen and Bat Masterson would like to bet $5,000 against the even-money wagers that Corbett wins in twenty rounds, and Allen said he fancied Mitchell but would not bet a cent on him after seeing the two men before the fight.
Tom Allen played a joke on a newspaper reporter in January 1894, leaving him waiting at Mitchell's training quarters while the trainers took a nap.

In January 1894 Tom Allen wrote to Fred Watkins that Mitchell could not lose and was in the pink of condition, and that odds of 2 to 1 might be obtainable at the ringside; a letter reported by Alderman Cronin said Mitchell was fit to fight for a kingdom.
Tom Allen found a porpoise struggling in the shallow water on the beach at the training camp, tried to keep it away, and then reported to the training party how he had captured it.
Tom Allen lost a diamond ring on the train home from Jacksonville and later found it by the glitter of a piece of wire from a beer bottle.
Tom Allen said there was no fight between Corbett and Mitchell.
Tom Allen said he thoroughly believed Corbett could whip any pugilist, including Peter Jackson and Ed Smith.
In December 1894 Tom Allen and Tom Kelly doubted that Bob Fitzsimmons could fight successfully with his arms or wrists.

In a letter to the Post-Dispatch on 23 December 1894 Tom Allen said Andy Bowen's seconds should have thrown up the sponge three rounds before Bowen was knocked out by George Lavigne, and that prize fighting should be held in the open air and boxing would survive the closing of the New Orleans clubs.
On 11 January 1895 Tom Allen said no fight could be pulled off around St. Louis at that time, and advised Neist to try for a wrestling match with Mooney.
In May 1895 Tom Allen and his old backer Fred Watkins were regular patrons of the races at the St. Louis Fair Grounds.
In November 1895 Tom Allen was among the old-time pugilists missing from the Hot Springs gathering.
In February 1896 Tom Allen said he did not know the first principle of bull fighting, but believed any so-called sport that calls for dead horses and bulls is no sport at all.
In September 1896 Tom Allen hung a picture of William McKinley on the wall of Champion's Rest among the best pugs and wrestlers, and backed him for president against Cleveland.
In November 1896 Tom Allen was in close conference with Peter Maher during the Maher and Choynski fight and had a reserved seat at the ringside.
Tom Allen said Frank Slavin's defeat by Bob Armstrong could not have ended any other way, given Slavin's condition.
On 21 January 1897 Tom Allen and Tom Kelly, at the Post-Dispatch's request, watched Jim Corbett at a Havlin's Theater matinee and declared him fit to fight.
In February 1897 the paper described Tom Allen as an enthusiastic Corbett man, and Allen said Corbett was the fastest big man he had ever seen in the ring and would beat Fitzsimmons quickly.

In June 1897 Paddy Smith, his brother Denver Ed Smith and Ike Weir, the Belfast Spider, stayed at Tom Allen's place in St. Louis while looking for fights, and Denver Ed Smith shook hands with Allen and had breakfast there on 14 June.
On 15 June 1897 Tom Allen of St. Louis offered to back Denver Ed Smith to the extent of $2,000 for a return fight with Joe Choynski or Joe Goddard, if Smith could arrange one.
After seeing the Derby run at the Fair Grounds in St. Louis on Saturday 26 June 1897, Tom Allen began going to the races there.
On 29 December 1897 Tom Allen commented on Fitzsimmons and said Corbett should take Fitzsimmons at his word.
On 26 February 1899 Allen had been drinking heavily and was still under the influence of liquor when he was moved to the Four Courts.
In March 1900 Tom Allen was rough and surly with most people but kind and gentle with his daughter.
Tom Allen sold property on the south side of Geyer Avenue, between Ninth and Tenth streets, to Henry Steinmeyer for $2,500 in February 1901.
Tom Allen's will, made a few weeks before his death, left his estate, except $20, to Tillie Hartgrove; it was witnessed by Dr. Heine Marks and Dr. C. A. Newcomb and filed for probate in April 1903.

In early April 1903 friends of Allen said strangers were trying to get his property by taking advantage of his mental condition; his horse and buggy and a safety deposit box, from which $500 was reportedly taken, were said to be targeted.
Public Administrator Garrard Strode took charge of the estate of Thomas Allen, the late saloonkeeper and former prize fighter, on April 8, 1903.
Tillie Hartgrove stood on the other side of Tom Allen's coffin at the funeral in April 1903.
On April 11, 1903 R. W. L. Gillespie said Allen left no estate, as was generally supposed.
In June 1903 Market Street believed the spirit of Tom Allen was ringing the bell behind the bar at Champion's Rest.

In July 1903 Tillie Hartgrove, Allen's housekeeper, claimed the silk hat worn by "Lord" Barrington as property of the Allen estate; Barrington returned the hat by messenger, and it was put on display for Allen's friends with the silver cup he won in 1878.
The estate inventory of Tom Allen's property listed a champion's cup and shade, a barrel of whisky and other goods, on July 28, 1903.
Allen's silver cup was retrieved from a Market Street pawn shop in 1938 by the father of Thomas Allen Taylor, and in 1978 it was in the home of his great-grandson Thomas Allen Taylor.
